title: Shelf-stable, broadly compatible replacement for critical blood functions

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a practical substitute for two critical blood functions during acute resuscitation: carrying oxygen to tissues and helping stop bleeding. It would combine clinically effective performance with useful storage life, reliable manufacturing, and compatibility across a defined range of recipients. Oxygen-carrying and hemostatic components could be separate products, provided each component and their intended combined use are validated. The NIH SEED guide provides the underlying functional distinction by treating oxygen carriers and platelet substitutes as separate development areas.

Scope definition: this is a proposed replacement for selected blood functions over a clinically useful emergency treatment period. It does not require reproducing blood's infection-fighting functions or sustaining a person indefinitely without donor blood. Here, shelf stability means retaining specified quality, safety, and functional performance for a validated duration under defined storage conditions. Broad compatibility means suitability across a specified recipient population, with any exclusions made explicit.

significance.text: If safe and effective products could be manufactured reliably and distributed with practical storage requirements, they could make lifesaving resuscitation available when suitable donor blood is unavailable. Oxygen delivery and bleeding control address distinct immediate needs after substantial blood loss; achieving both could expand the circumstances in which emergency teams can provide effective support. The guide describes the potential life-sustaining role of substitutes, including oxygen carriers for emergencies and low blood supply, and platelet substitutes intended to help stop bleeding. These are reasons the capability could matter, rather than evidence that the proposed survival benefit has already been achieved.

Conditional downstream possibilities include keeping useful resuscitation supplies closer to emergencies and reducing dependence on timely access to compatible donor products for the functions successfully replaced. Those benefits would depend on actual storage conditions, ease of administration, manufacturing capacity, cost, and clinical performance. A product requiring difficult handling or benefiting only a narrow recipient group could remain valuable while delivering a smaller logistical breakthrough than the title suggests.

The analogy to a complete replacement for blood has important limits. The guide notes that the developments it discusses do not reproduce infection-fighting functions. Demonstrating oxygen transport or bleeding control would therefore establish a bounded therapeutic capability, and would not by itself show that all blood functions had been replaced. Immune replacement and indefinite substitution are outside this concept's proposed scope.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is clinically validated replacement of oxygen delivery and effective hemostasis together with practical storage and reproducible production. The guide supports these as distinct development objectives requiring further safety and efficacy validation, and discusses storage and manufacturing considerations. Making an oxygen carrier or a material intended to promote clotting is only part of the task: its performance must translate into useful patient outcomes within an appropriate treatment strategy.

Proposed engineering requirements include delivering enough oxygen safely during the intended treatment period and supporting bleeding control without provoking inappropriate clotting or other serious harm. Vascular toxicity is also a safety concern to evaluate. The supplied evidence does not establish these particular mechanisms as observed adverse events in substitute trials; they are safety constraints for the proposed innovation. Separate components would additionally require evidence that their doses, timing, and biological effects remain safe and effective when used together.

Proposed practical barriers include preserving functional activity throughout storage, defining acceptable storage and transport conditions, maintaining consistent quality between manufacturing batches, and establishing which recipients can safely receive the product. Compatibility cannot remain an undefined promise: development must identify relevant exclusions and limits. These requirements must be achieved together, because a storage advantage cannot compensate for inadequate clinical performance, and clinical efficacy alone does not establish distributability.

current_state.text: The NIH SEED Regulatory Knowledge Guide for Blood and Blood Products, updated February 2024, describes oxygen carriers and platelet substitutes as separate development areas requiring safety and efficacy validation. It discusses hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers for potential emergency use and platelet substitutes for bleeding control. It also states that developments discussed there did not replicate blood's infection-fighting functions. This establishes the historical development categories and their intended roles; it does not establish successful replacement of the combined functions proposed here.

The guide states that no FDA-approved oxygen-carrying blood substitute was commercially available at the time covered by its February 2024 update. That statement concerns a particular regulatory and commercial scope. It does not establish the absence of experimental demonstrations worldwide, resolve the status of hemostatic substitutes, or determine whether a product or combination subsequently demonstrated the proposed capability.

The supplied evidence does not establish the development landscape as of November 1, 2026, the reference date used in the review. No updated product inventory, bounded freshness-search results, or product-specific clinical outcome data were supplied. Consequently, the earlier present-tense assertion that no single product has demonstrated this broad replacement cannot be retained as a verified current fact. The remaining gap is uncertainty about recent evidence, rather than evidence that later achievements are absent or false.

The supplied review reports complete text coverage of all 23 pages of the guide, without reported extraction truncation; figures were not inspected. Its relevant judgments rely on prose, especially section 3.2 and the storage and manufacturing discussions. The source index records retrieval on November 11, 2026, but retrieval does not update the guide's February 2024 content. The guide is a regulatory overview, and the supplied material does not provide the product-level data needed to compare efficacy, adverse events, shelf life, compatibility, or manufacturing performance quantitatively.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: controlled trials in relevant emergency settings should show survival and safety comparable to an appropriate blood-product strategy, using prespecified, clinically justified comparison margins. Trials should define the recipient population, treatment period, dosing, accompanying care, and rescue treatment. Evidence should establish clinically useful oxygen delivery and bleeding control within that strategy. These are proposed criteria for assessing this concept, not established standards or a trial design endorsed by the supplied guide.
completion_criteria.label: Emergency trials demonstrate survival and safety comparable to blood products

completion_criteria.text: Proposed component and combination demonstration: if oxygen-carrying and hemostatic functions are supplied separately, each component should have evidence supporting its intended use, and the combined regimen should be evaluated directly. Component successes alone would not establish that their joint use delivers comparable outcomes or acceptable safety. Assessment should address serious harms, including vascular effects and inappropriate clotting, without presuming that the supplied evidence has already documented these effects.
completion_criteria.label: Separate components and combined regimen demonstrate intended-use effectiveness and safety

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical demonstration: establish a useful shelf life under explicitly stated storage and transport conditions, with retained functional performance and acceptable quality through the claimed expiration period. Reproducible manufacturing should be demonstrated across batches and at a scale relevant to intended deployment. Compatibility claims should identify the populations studied, contraindications, exclusions, and administration requirements. Numerical shelf-life targets and performance margins remain to be justified rather than assumed.
completion_criteria.label: Claimed shelf life retains functional performance and acceptable quality

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundaries: convincing evidence should include confirmation across independent clinical settings and reproducible manufacturing and storage results. The resulting claim should state the treatment duration, recipient groups, emergency contexts, and blood functions actually demonstrated. Finite testing can establish broad performance across those conditions; it cannot establish literal compatibility with every recipient or effectiveness in every emergency.
completion_criteria.label: Independent confirmation reproduces clinical, manufacturing, and storage results

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: BME-13, Durable autonomous artificial-organ replacement, shares the aim of replacing a physiological function through engineered technology. BME-14 concerns selected circulating blood functions during acute treatment, while BME-13 emphasizes durable, autonomous replacement of an organ. Success in one would not establish the operating duration or functional breadth required by the other.

Roster-based synthesis: BME-01, Manufacturing transplantable human organs on demand, and BME-12, Reliable, scalable animal-to-human organ transplantation, overlap with BME-14 in the importance of compatibility, reproducible supply, and clinical validation. They provide transplantable organs through different approaches; BME-14 provides selected blood functions. BME-06, Long-term banking of transplantable human organs, shares a preservation and distribution challenge, but storing functional organs and storing blood substitutes require distinct demonstrations.

Roster-based synthesis: BME-08, Reliable, antigen-specific immune tolerance, is relevant to questions of biological compatibility. Broad compatibility for a blood substitute would not itself demonstrate antigen-specific immune tolerance, and immune tolerance would not supply oxygen transport or bleeding control. BME-05, Programmable living medicines that sense and respond inside the body, could overlap if a substitute used responsive living components, but BME-14 does not require a living or programmable product.

Roster-based synthesis: BME-09, Physiological extra-uterine support through extreme prematurity, may share needs for oxygen delivery and careful physiological support, but its developmental setting and broader support requirements are distinct from acute blood replacement. BME-18, Long-lived continuous sensing of multiple clinically useful biomarkers, could help monitor treatment effects; sensing would remain a complementary capability rather than a replacement for oxygen-carrying or hemostatic function.

change_log.reason: Evidence for individual oxygen-carrying and hemostatic products would not establish the safety and efficacy of a combined regimen.

change_log.reason: The review found support for general safety validation, but not for those specific trial findings.

change_log.change: Made proposed completion criteria assessable through justified comparison margins, defined storage conditions, recipient scope, manufacturing consistency, and reproducibility.
change_log.reason: These additions clarify what would constitute convincing evidence while preserving their status as proposals rather than published consensus.

change_log.reason: These limitations affect interpretation and prevent retrieval date from being mistaken for evidence currency.

unresolved_issues: The supplied material does not resolve product, trial, regulatory, or demonstration status after the guide's February 2024 update, including status as of November 1, 2026.
No product-specific quantitative evidence was supplied for survival, serious adverse events, oxygen delivery, bleeding control, shelf life, compatibility, or manufacturing scale.
Clinically justified comparison margins, storage-duration targets, recipient populations, treatment duration, and emergency settings remain to be specified.
The supplied evidence does not establish whether vascular toxicity or inappropriate clotting occurred in particular substitute trials, or how those risks differ between approaches.
Whether separate oxygen-carrying and hemostatic products can meet the proposed criteria when used together remains unresolved.
Figures were not inspected in the supplied review; the retained conclusions rely on the reviewed prose.

brief.title: Storable blood substitutes for emergency care
possible: After severe blood loss, people could receive emergency treatment that carries oxygen to their tissues and helps stop bleeding when suitable donor blood is unavailable.
Emergency teams could keep supplies closer to where people need them. The treatment could use separate products for these functions, with storage conditions and recipient limits clearly defined.
why: Blood loss creates distinct needs: getting oxygen to tissues and stopping further bleeding. Replacing both functions could help emergency teams sustain people who cannot promptly receive suitable donor blood.
Reliable production and practical storage could reduce dependence on timely blood donations for these functions.

sources.showed: Their regulatory guide describes products being developed to carry oxygen and substitutes for platelets, the blood components that help stop bleeding. It explains the need to establish safety, effectiveness and manufacturing quality.
sources.cited_for: The guide supports treating oxygen delivery and bleeding control as separate development goals.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate a treatment that combines both functions with useful storage life and broad recipient compatibility.

shown: Developers are pursuing oxygen carriers and platelet substitutes as separate approaches. The NIH SEED guide describes their intended roles, but reports no clinical demonstration of the full combined capability.
missing: Clinical trials must establish useful oxygen delivery and bleeding control, with survival and safety comparable to appropriate blood treatment.
Separate products need evidence that their combined doses, timing and effects remain safe and effective.
Products must retain function through their claimed storage life and be manufactured consistently at a useful scale.
Studies must establish which recipients can safely receive treatment and which require exclusions.

milestones.label: Emergency trials show comparable survival and safety
milestones.explanation: Controlled emergency trials would have to show survival and safety comparable to appropriate blood treatment, using justified comparison limits. This would establish that oxygen delivery and bleeding control translate into patient benefit.

milestones.label: Separate products work safely together
milestones.explanation: If functions come from separate products, each would need evidence for its intended use, and their combined use would need direct testing. Success separately would not establish safe, effective treatment together.

milestones.label: Stored products retain function and consistent quality
milestones.explanation: Testing would have to establish retained function through the claimed shelf life, consistent production at useful scale and defined recipient limits. These results would establish practical storage, supply and compatibility.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results across defined conditions
milestones.explanation: Independent settings would have to confirm clinical, manufacturing and storage results within stated treatment and recipient limits. This would establish how broadly the capability holds.

uncertain: Whether separate oxygen carriers and bleeding-control products can meet the clinical goals together remains unresolved.
Acceptable clinical comparison limits, storage duration, treatment period and recipient groups still need definition.
The risks of blood-vessel harm and unwanted clotting, and how they differ between approaches, remain open questions.

page.title: Shelf-stable blood analog system
page.definition: A blood analog system uses substitutes for red cells and platelets, with plasma, to provide oxygen transport, hemostasis (bleeding control) and circulating-volume support after blood loss. Its components work together and retain function through validated storage without continuous refrigeration.

goal.need: NIH’s February 2024 guide specifies refrigerated red-cell storage for up to 42 days and platelet storage usually limited to five days with constant agitation. These components supply oxygen transport and bleeding control. Replacing their functions in a resuscitation regimen that does not require continuous refrigeration addresses distinct storage and handling constraints.

statements.body: Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, FSHARP programme
statements.quote: The primary problem FSHARP aims to solve is whole blood’s dependence on cold chain and resupply.

statements.body: U.S. Department of Defense, Combat Readiness–Medical Research Program
statements.quote: developing a dried, whole-blood surrogate that can address logistical challenges related to the availability of whole blood in austere battlefield environments.
statements.context: Describes its funded project combining ErythroMer, SynthoPlate and freeze-dried plasma.

completion.title: FDA authorizes a shelf-stable blood analog system for traumatic hemorrhage.
completion.criterion: FDA issues an Emergency Use Authorization or full approval/licensure covering combined use of an oxygen carrier, a hemostatic component and plasma for trauma/hemorrhage resuscitation. The authorized presentation meets FSHARP’s storage target: six months at 4, 25 and 40 °C with ≤10% functional loss. Recipient eligibility, dosing and conditions of use are those authorized by FDA.
completion.set_by: DARPA: RAPIID announcement of 28 May 2026 and TA-3 programme announcement, Section 1.3; FSHARP solicitation, Table 2.
completion.threshold_quote: The ultimate goal is to deliver a fully FDA-authorized, deployable system capable of saving lives at the point of injury
completion.basis: RAPIID identifies FDA authorization of the integrated system as its endpoint and includes EUA or full licensure. FSHARP supplies the numerical storage specification. Applying these requirements to the combined regimen distinguishes system authorization from authorization of an individual component.

milestones.title: A whole blood analog reaches 60% of stored blood function in three laboratory domains.
milestones.criterion: Reach FSHARP’s first-year benchmark of 60% of stored blood performance for oxygenation, hemostasis and hemodynamics (blood flow and pressure). CWRU reported reaching the hemostasis benchmark for the programme year ending in January 2024; sample sizes and results for the other two domains were not supplied. This institutional report is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: DARPA’s FSHARP programme, intermediate targets reported by Case Western Reserve University, a programme developer, in its spring 2024 newsletter.
milestones.threshold_quote: 60% functionality at the end of year one

milestones.title: A blood analog matches whole blood within 10% in large-animal hemorrhage and complex-trauma tests.
milestones.criterion: In large animals, demonstrate a combined formulation within 10% of whole blood for hemodynamics, oxygenation and hemostasis, with no increase in safety anomalies. Test hemorrhage alone, hemorrhage with traumatic brain injury, and hemorrhage with trauma-induced coagulopathy (disordered clotting). FSHARP requires third-party validation. DARPA reported programme proof of concept on 28 May 2026 without sample sizes or comparative results; that announcement is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, FSHARP solicitation HR001121S0027, Sections 1.2.1 and 1.2.3 and Table 1.
milestones.threshold_quote: within 10% of whole blood function in head-to-head comparison for hemodynamic measures, oxygenation, and hemostasis.

milestones.title: Blood analog components retain function for six months and reach production of 300 units per week.
milestones.criterion: Meet RAPIID Phase 1 Table 2: ≥6 months at sustained 4, 25 and 40 °C, with ≤10% difference from fresh product in physicochemical characteristics and function; ≥3 months under those conditions in government-chosen packaging; reconstitution within five minutes after storage at 4 °C in that packaging; and production of 300 units/week, each unit a discrete administered item. Partial evidence published on 20 April 2026: Lyo-SP retained size and charge for 360 days at 4 and approximately 25 °C; assays were performed at least in triplicate. These component measurements do not establish the complete system target.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, RAPIID solicitation DARPA-PS-26-124, Amendment 01, Section 2.3.2.1, Table 2; the complete numerical specification is tabulated.

milestones.title: A participant receives the combined blood analog under an effective FDA Investigational New Drug application.
milestones.criterion: Administer the combined blood analog to a participant under an effective Investigational New Drug application (IND) and required ethics approvals. An IND takes effect 30 days after FDA receipt without a clinical hold, or earlier on FDA notification. A 2022 Japanese component trial administered 10–100 mL hemoglobin vesicles to 11 healthy men; one infusion stopped after rash. It did not administer a combined blood analog.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.40; DARPA’s RAPIID TA-3 announcement, Section 1.6.3, specifies initiation of a Phase I trial of the blood analog.
milestones.threshold_quote: An investigator may not administer an investigational new drug to human subjects until the IND goes into effect under paragraph (b) of this section.

milestones.title: A blood analog is non-inferior to stored whole blood for safety in a Phase I clinical trial.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate clinical safety non-inferiority of the combined blood analog to stored whole blood in Phase I. The programme document supplies no numerical clinical margin or sample size; its Phase 2 targets are subject to revision.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, RAPIID TA-3 announcement DARPA-PA-26-09, Section 1.6.3, Table 4; the safety non-inferiority threshold appears in the table.

milestones.title: A blood analog is non-inferior to stored whole blood for safety and efficacy in a Phase II clinical trial.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate safety and efficacy non-inferiority of the combined blood analog to stored whole blood in Phase II. The published programme target supplies no clinical endpoints, numerical margin or sample size and is subject to revision.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, RAPIID TA-3 announcement DARPA-PA-26-09, Section 1.6.3, Table 4.
milestones.threshold_quote: Demonstrate non-inferiority to stored whole blood safety & efficacy in Phase II clinical trial
